Chapter 9: Accountability and Real Change—What It Really Takes
So, here’s a question that comes up again and again—can a controlling partner really change? I wish the answer were simple, but it’s not. The truth is, real change is rare. It takes a lot more than promises or good intentions. It actually means a person has to fundamentally shift the way they see themselves, and the people around them.
Let me share a story. There was this man who, after years of trying to control his partner, finally agreed to join a program focused on abusive behavior. In the beginning, he just went through the motions—showing up, saying all the right things, even apologizing. But it wasn’t until someone challenged him to really confront his own sense of entitlement that things started to move.
He talked about how uncomfortable it was to realize just how much he’d relied on power and control to get what he wanted. Admitting that wasn’t easy, and honestly, the process was slow. There were setbacks, moments where he got defensive, and times he wanted to give up. But little by little, he started to see his partner differently—as an equal, someone who deserved respect and the freedom to make her own choices.
But here’s something to notice: most people don’t get this far. A lot of controlling partners aren’t willing to give up the advantages that come with power. Sure, they might go to therapy or counseling, but if they’re not focusing on accountability and really changing their core beliefs, those old patterns just keep coming back.
For people who genuinely want to change, specialized intervention programs work better than traditional couples counseling or anger management. These programs are all about challenging those attitudes of entitlement, helping participants learn empathy, and holding them responsible for their actions. Progress isn’t measured by what they say—it’s measured by whether their actions are consistently respectful over time.
So, if you ever hear promises of quick fixes, or notice superficial changes, be careful. Real transformation doesn’t happen overnight. It takes ongoing effort, and a real commitment to growth. If you’re on the receiving end of controlling behavior, your safety and well-being have to come first. Don’t put your life on hold waiting for someone else to change.
Accountability also means being willing to face the consequences of your actions. Sometimes, that involves legal steps, separation, or setting clear boundaries. It’s not about punishing someone—it’s about creating the right conditions for actual growth and healing.
In the end, the choice to change belongs to the controlling partner. No one else can do the work for them. And if you’re someone seeking freedom from control, your most important step is to focus on your own needs, your dreams, and reclaiming your sense of self. That’s where real healing begins.
